title: Say it out loud (1:1)
hookLine: return includes spoken confession: I did this, I regret it, I won't again
tomorrow: you said sorry. how would you ever know you've really changed?

cards: You type sorry. You delete it. You type sorry about the other day.
Delete. You feel it, honestly, all the way down. So isn't feeling sorry enough?
Maimonides' answer is short: no. Feeling is where it starts, but the return isn't finished inside your chest. It has to come out as words.
In Hebrew that spoken confession has a name: vidui.

teach.b: The question: what does real return need? Here is Maimonides' answer, in plain words.

teach.h: I DID THIS. I REGRET. NOT AGAIN.
teach.b: The confession goes like this: please, God, I have sinned, I have done wrong before You, and I did this, naming it. And I regret it, and I'm ashamed of what I did, and I will never go back to this.
He calls that the heart of vidui, and says whoever says more is praised. Three moves: I did this. I regret it.
I won't again. And notice the middle of the first one: naming it. Not sorry for everything.
In Islam, the scholar al-Nawawi, in his collection Riyad as-Salihin, teaches that turning back to God, tawbah, has conditions: stop the wrong, regret it, and resolve never to return to it.
And if the wrong was against a person, make it right with them. Shared ground: the same three moves, almost word for word. Stop, regret, resolve.
Two traditions that honor many of the same prophets also share a map of coming home. And an honest difference. Nawawi's conditions live in the heart and the deed, between the person and God.
Maimonides adds that the return must also be said out loud, the deed named in words.
Here's something to tell a friend tonight: on Yom Kippur, the community says a long vidui together, in the plural, ashamnu, we have been guilty, so nobody has to stand up and say it alone.

how: Vidui is said in the Yom Kippur prayers, many times, and in some communities in daily prayers; Maimonides' own short formula is a model for private confession before God.

o: a list of sins chanted by a cantor alone
a silent feeling of guilt kept deep in the heart
spoken confession: naming the deed, regret, resolve

games.q: the shape of vidui, and a neighbor's — tap the pairs.

s: for Maimonides, a general 'sorry for everything' is enough
the confession names the deed: I did this.
al-Nawawi's conditions for tawbah include regret and a resolve not to return
stop, regret, resolve, and make it right with anyone you wronged.
Judaism and Islam teach return in exactly the same way
they share the three moves; Maimonides adds that the return is spoken aloud.

games.q: your brother broke your headphones and says, 'my bad, whatever happened, sorry.' what's missing, by Maimonides' outline?
o: naming it: I broke your headphones, I regret it, I won't again.
nothing: any sorry counts as long as he means it inside.
a gift: words never count without something to make up for it.
games.why: vidui names the deed, says the regret, and resolves not to return. 'whatever happened' skips the first step.

practice: Find a quiet spot and choose one small thing to come back from. Following Maimonides' outline, say three short sentences softly out loud: I did this, naming it. I regret it.
I won't again. Then sit in the quiet the words leave behind.

wordCard.voice: Vidui. Spoken confession: the deed named out loud, with regret and a resolve not to return to it.

orig.note: Hebrew: confession, spoken aloud. Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1.

carryVoice: Your line: say it out loud, and name the thing. Two of thirty in the laws of return.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Hilchot Teshuvah 1:1 (the confession formula: I have sinned… I did such-and-such… I regret and am ashamed… I will never return to this; one who adds is praiseworthy)
al-Nawawi, Riyad as-Salihin, Book of Repentance (chapter on tawbah, opening: the conditions of repentance)
Yom Kippur liturgy: the vidui (Ashamnu), said in the plural
